chmmc-2015-power-01a.prompt: The sum of two independent $6$-sided dice rolls is a random variable $D_2$ with outcomes in the range $2\le n\le12$. What is the expected value of $D_2$?

chmmc-2015-power-01b.prompt: A *counting random variable* $X$ samples a random process and returns a positive integer; $\Pr(X=n)$ is the probability that it returns $n$, and its expected value is $\mathbb EX=\sum_{n}n\cdot\Pr(X=n)$. For counting random variables $X$ and $Y$, let $X+Y$ be the result of sampling $X$, sampling $Y$, and summing the results, so that $$\Pr(X+Y=n)=\sum_{k\le n}\Pr(X=k\text{ and }Y=n-k).$$ Prove that the expected value of $X+Y$ is the sum of the expected values of $X$ and $Y$ (linearity of expectation).
chmmc-2015-power-01b.answer: $\mathbb E(X+Y)=\sum_{j,k}(j+k)\Pr(X=k,Y=j)=\mathbb EX+\mathbb EY$ by splitting the sum and summing out the other variable.

chmmc-2015-power-01c.prompt: Using linearity of expectation (the expected value of a sum of random variables is the sum of their expected values), compute the expected value of the total outcome of rolling ten $6$-sided dice.

chmmc-2015-power-02a.prompt: In a chess tournament with $n$ participants, every pair plays one match and each match has a winner and a loser. The outcome of the tournament is the list of results of all matches. Call an outcome *$k$-good* if for every choice of $k$ participants there is a single participant who won against all $k$ of them. Show that for any $n>k>0$ there is an outcome of a tournament with $n$ participants that is not $k$-good.
chmmc-2015-power-02a.answer: Let one player win all games and take a set of $k$ players containing him: nobody beat him, so nobody beat all of them.

chmmc-2015-power-02b.prompt: In a chess tournament with $n$ participants, every pair plays one match and each match has a winner and a loser. The outcome of the tournament is the list of results of all matches. Call an outcome *$k$-good* if for every choice of $k$ participants there is a single participant who won against all $k$ of them. Suppose $n=3$ and $k=1$. Explicitly describe a $1$-good outcome of a tournament with $3$ participants.

chmmc-2015-power-02c.prompt: Decide the outcome of a $n$-participant tournament by a fair coin flip for each of the $\binom n2$ games (independently). Fix a set of $k$ participants, and let $P_{n,k}$ be the probability that no participant won against all $k$ of them. Calculate $P_{n,k}$.

chmmc-2015-power-02d.prompt: Decide the outcome of an $n$-participant tournament by fair coin flips, one for each game. Let $P_{n,k}=(1-2^{-k})^{n-k}$ be the probability that, for a fixed set of $k$ participants, nobody won against all $k$ of them. Prove that if $\binom nkP_{n,k}<1$, then the probability that the random outcome is $k$-good is nonzero. (You may use $\Pr(A\text{ or }B)\le\Pr(A)+\Pr(B)$.)
chmmc-2015-power-02d.answer: Union bound over the $\binom nk$ sets of size $k$: $\Pr(\text{not }k\text{-good})\le\binom nkP_{n,k}<1$.

chmmc-2015-power-02e.prompt: Decide the outcome of an $n$-participant tournament by fair coin flips, one for each game. Let $P_{n,k}=(1-2^{-k})^{n-k}$ be the probability that, for a fixed set of $k$ participants, nobody won against all $k$ of them. Conclude that if $\binom nkP_{n,k}<1$, then there exists a $k$-good outcome for a tournament with $n$ participants.
chmmc-2015-power-02e.answer: A positive probability means at least one of the $2^{\binom n2}$ equally likely outcomes is $k$-good.

chmmc-2015-power-02f.prompt: Decide the outcome of an $n$-participant tournament by fair coin flips, one for each game. Let $P_{n,k}=(1-2^{-k})^{n-k}$ be the probability that, for a fixed set of $k$ participants, nobody won against all $k$ of them. Prove that for every fixed $k$ there is a sufficiently large $n$ such that a $k$-good tournament with $n$ participants exists. (Hint: show $\binom nkP_{n,k}<1$ has a solution $n$.)
chmmc-2015-power-02f.answer: $\binom nk(1-2^{-k})^{n-k}\le n^ke^{-(n-k)/2^k}\to0$, so it is $<1$ for large $n$.

chmmc-2015-power-03a.prompt: An adversary places $n$ dots (points) on a piece of paper (the plane). You then place $n$ unit-radius coins (disks) on the paper, with disjoint interiors (they may touch on the boundary). You win if every dot is covered by a coin. Prove, using elementary methods, that you can always win if $n=3$.
chmmc-2015-power-03a.answer: If all distances are $\ge2$, center a disk on each dot. Otherwise cover a close pair by one disk and place a second disk, tangent-or-farther, over the third dot.

chmmc-2015-power-03b.prompt: Suppose we have infinitely many unit-radius disks and want to cover the whole plane as efficiently as we know how: we tile the plane with regular hexagons of side length $2$, and put a disk of unit radius at each vertex and at each hexagon's center (see the picture; disks at the vertices of a hexagon are shared with the neighbouring hexagons). What fraction of each hexagon is covered by the disks?

chmmc-2015-power-03c.prompt: There are $10$ points in the plane. You lay down an infinite hexagonal tiling with side length $2$ with a hexagon centered at the origin. Next you pick a point $P$ uniformly at random inside the hexagon at the origin and translate the whole grid so that the center of that hexagon is at $P$. Finally you place unit disks at all vertices and centers of the translated tiling (as in the covering by disks where each hexagon has a disk at each vertex and at its center). Calculate the expected number of the $10$ points that are covered by your disks, and justify your answer.

chmmc-2015-power-03d.prompt: An adversary places $n$ dots (points) on a piece of paper (the plane). You then place $n$ unit-radius coins (disks) on the paper, with disjoint interiors (they may touch on the boundary). You win if every dot is covered by a coin. Given that the expected value in the previous problem (the expected number of the $10$ points covered by a random shift of the disk-hexagon pattern) is strictly greater than $9$, argue that with $n=10$ you can always cover all $10$ dots with $10$ non-overlapping unit disks.
chmmc-2015-power-03d.answer: Some shift covers all 10 points (otherwise the expectation is $\le9$); only 10 of its disks are needed.
